Where is Albuquerque and how is it laid out?

Albuquerque is the county seat of Bernalillo County and the most populous city in New Mexico. According to Wikipedia, it lies in the Albuquerque Basin, with the Sandia Mountains to the east, the West Mesa to the west, and the Rio Grande and its bosque running north to south through the middle.

Elevation changes a lot inside the city limits. Wikipedia gives a range from about 4,900 feet near the river to more than 6,700 feet in foothill areas such as Sandia Heights. A house in the valley and a house in the foothills can face different weather, views and insurance questions even when they are a few miles apart.

The city was founded in 1706 as La Villa de Alburquerque, an outpost on El Camino Real. The 2020 Census counted 564,559 residents, and the Census Bureau estimate on this page is 556,588 for July 1, 2025.

Wikipedia counts more than 160 sites in the city on the National Register of Historic Places, and lists the Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta and the New Mexico State Fair among its annual events. A seller of an older property near a historic site should ask the city whether any extra review applies before planning exterior work.

What drives the Albuquerque economy?

Federal research, defense, higher education and health care anchor it. Wikipedia calls Albuquerque New Mexico's principal economic center and the heart of the New Mexico Technology Corridor, with Sandia National Laboratories and Kirtland Air Force Base among the federal installations.

  • The University of New Mexico is the state's flagship and largest university, and Central New Mexico Community College is also in the city.
  • Health care names include Presbyterian Health Services and the Lovelace Respiratory Research Institute.
  • Intel has a fabrication site in neighboring Rio Rancho, and Wikipedia lists a Facebook data center in Los Lunas.

Kirtland is described as the largest installation in the Air Force Global Strike Command. Federal and university jobs tend to bring relocations, which means sellers who are transferring out and buyers who need to move quickly both show up in the Albuquerque market. We do not have a sourced figure for how many sales that involves, so we do not state one.

How do roads, rail and the airport affect a sale?

The Albuquerque International Sunport is about 3 miles southeast of the central business district, according to Wikipedia; Wikipedia also shows an I-25 bridge among the city's crossings. The New Mexico Rail Runner Express began service in July 2006 and now connects Santa Fe, Sandoval, Bernalillo and Valencia Counties with thirteen stops, three of them in Albuquerque.

Commute and airport access are things a buyer will ask about, so a seller can mention them. For an owner who has already moved to another state, the same facts argue for a sale that does not require traveling back for showings or repairs.

What is Albuquerque's climate and how does it affect a house?

Albuquerque has a cold semi-arid climate. Wikipedia notes that average annual precipitation is less than half of evaporation, and that no month has a daily mean temperature below freezing. Moisture is limited, and the Sandia Mountains create a rain shadow over much of the city, though the mountains themselves get about 10 to 17 inches annually by one estimate on that page.

For a house, this usually means:

  • Roof and stucco wear from strong sun, more than from rain.
  • Evaporative cooling and heating systems that age quickly with year-round use.
  • Foothill and East Mountain homes seeing more snow than the valley, which can matter for roofs and access roads.

None of this blocks a sale. It does mean a buyer's inspector will go through the roof, cooling unit and stucco, and any of those can trigger a repair request that a cash purchase avoids.

When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?

The Bernalillo County Treasurer lists November 10 as the due date for the first half and April 10 as the due date for the second half. Late fees begin to accrue on the first-half balance on December 10, according to the Treasurer's FAQ.

The county's October 2026 announcement says that for 2026 bills the second half is due April 10, 2027, and becomes delinquent if not paid on or before May 10, 2027. Property owners get an additional month after November 10 before first-half taxes are considered late.

The Bernalillo County Assessor values the house and the Treasurer bills and collects. The city of Albuquerque does not send its own property tax bill. If you sell during the tax year, the closing agent splits what is owed and pays it from your proceeds.

What city rules should an Albuquerque seller know about?

Albuquerque land use runs through the Integrated Development Ordinance, or IDO, which the City Council updated in 2025. The Planning Department handles questions and can be reached at 505-924-3860.

One rule that comes up with older properties is the accessory dwelling unit, which the city calls a casita. The city's page says only one casita is allowed per lot in R-A and R-1 zones. If you have a guest house or converted garage, confirm that it was built with a permit and counts as a legal unit before you advertise it as an extra bedroom or rental.

Unpermitted additions are a common negotiating point in any sale, though we have not seen Albuquerque-specific numbers on how often. A buyer using a loan may ask for them to be legalized. A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands.

What are your options for selling a house in Albuquerque?

You can list, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer. The choice comes down to how much time, repair money and certainty you have.

  • Traditional listing: broad exposure, with commission, repairs, appraisal and loan approval before closing.
  • For sale by owner: keeps commission, but you carry the marketing and paperwork.
  • Cash sale to us: as-is purchase, no commission, no repair requests, and a closing date set around your schedule.

We do not promise a price. The offer depends on condition, location and what repairs the house needs, and it will usually be lower than a fully renovated retail sale. If you are carrying back tax, a probate property, a tenant you want to hand over, or a house that needs work you cannot afford, a cash route can be simpler. The title company handles the closing and pays off any mortgage, lien or tax from proceeds.

More questions about Albuquerque, NM

Who collects property tax in Albuquerque?

The Bernalillo County Treasurer bills and collects it. The Bernalillo County Assessor sets the value. The city of Albuquerque does not issue a separate property tax bill.

When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 and late fees begin December 10. The second half is due April 10 and becomes delinquent after May 10.

How high is Albuquerque?

Wikipedia gives a range from about 4,900 feet near the Rio Grande to more than 6,700 feet in the foothills, so conditions vary by neighborhood.

Can I sell an Albuquerque house with a casita or guest house?

Yes. Confirm first that it was permitted. The city's page says one casita is allowed per lot in R-A and R-1 zones. A cash buyer can purchase the property as-is.

What is the biggest employer base around Albuquerque?

Federal research and defense, including Sandia National Laboratories and Kirtland Air Force Base, along with the University of New Mexico and health care, according to Wikipedia.

Do I have to make repairs before a cash sale in Albuquerque?

No. A cash purchase is as-is, so roof, cooling and stucco problems do not need to be fixed first.

Where is Las Cruces, and what is it known for?

Las Cruces is the county seat of Doña Ana County and the second most populous city in New Mexico, with 111,385 residents in the 2020 census. It lies in the Mesilla Valley along the Rio Grande, 225 miles south of Albuquerque and 42 miles northwest of El Paso.

The Organ Mountains rise about 10 miles to the east, and the Doña Ana, Robledo and Picacho peaks frame the other sides. The city covers 76.6 square miles at an elevation of about 3,908 feet. Wikipedia says the city lacks a true central business district because a 1960s urban renewal project removed much of the original downtown, so retail has gathered on the east side while the historic center sits around Main Street.

CountyDoña Ana County (county seat)Wikipedia
2020 census population111,385Wikipedia, citing the Census Bureau
City area76.6 square milesWikipedia, citing the Census Bureau
ElevationAbout 3,908 feetWikipedia
Settled1849; railroad arrived 1881Wikipedia
Annual precipitation (1991 to 2020)9.14 inchesNOAA data on Wikipedia

Who employs people in Las Cruces?

The federal government is the city's major employer, through White Sands Missile Range and the White Sands Test Facility, according to Wikipedia. The same source lists New Mexico State University, Las Cruces Public Schools, the City of Las Cruces, Memorial Medical Center, Walmart, MountainView Regional Medical Center, Doña Ana County, Doña Ana Community College, Addus HealthCare and NASA among major employers.

NMSU was founded in 1888 as an agricultural college and is the state's only land-grant university. Its main campus sits next to, but outside, the city limits. Spaceport America, which has corporate offices in Las Cruces, operates about 55 miles north of town.

  • New Mexico State University is a large local employer and a major presence in the city.
  • Wikipedia describes the White Sands jobs as high-paying and stable.
  • Wikipedia says an influx of out-of-state retirees has also added to population growth.

For a seller, a varied job base means a varied pool of possible buyers. A house on the east side and one near the historic downtown may attract different people.

What should a Las Cruces seller know about heat, monsoon storms and arroyos?

Las Cruces has a cool desert climate, with very light rain from October to June and heavy afternoon thunderstorms in late summer. Wikipedia reports light freezes on 69 nights a year on average, spring wind that can cause blowing dust, and summer stretches above 100 degrees. The record high is 110 degrees and the wettest year on record at NMSU was 1941, with 19.60 inches.

Arroyos, the dry streams that cut through the desert uplands on both sides of the valley, carry water after heavy thunderstorms. A house near an arroyo or in a low lot may see water in a monsoon season even though the annual total is small. Check the FEMA flood map for your address and keep any insurance history ready.

Inspection items that matter here:

  • Roof condition and drainage after monsoon rain
  • Cooling systems that have run through summers above 100 degrees
  • Stucco cracks and window seals exposed to sun and wind
  • Dust and filter condition in the HVAC system

What is the Las Cruces vacant and abandoned property ordinance?

Las Cruces requires owners of long-vacant buildings to register them each year and pay a fee that grows annually. The City Council adopted the ordinance to address long-term vacancies, reduce deterioration and nuisance conditions, and encourage owners to return properties to use.

The rule generally covers buildings or portions of buildings that have not been lawfully occupied or in operation for at least two consecutive years. New properties are excluded for 24 months after a certificate of occupancy. Residential properties other than multi-tenant pay the fees below, according to the city.

Property typeYear 1Year 2Year 3 and later
Residential, not multi-tenant$500$1,000$2,000
Commercial and qualifying multi-tenant$2,000$4,000$8,000

Owners can apply for exemptions, including for construction or rehabilitation, foreclosure redemption periods, secured properties in probate or ownership litigation, and active sale or lease marketing that meets pricing and marketing requirements. Exemptions need city approval, last 12 months and can be renewed once. A final vacancy assessment can be appealed in writing to the Community Development Director within 30 days. The city can be reached at Vacancy@LasCruces.gov or 575-541-2299.

This matters to inherited and empty houses. If a Las Cruces house has sat empty close to two years, ask the city how registration and the fee apply before you list or sign a contract.

How does Las Cruces handle nuisance properties and code enforcement?

The city has adopted the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, which sets minimum standards for use, occupancy and upkeep of residential, non-residential, vacant and boarded buildings. A Nuisance Abatement Team made up of Code Enforcement, Community Development, Fire, Legal, Police and other departments works on problem properties.

Residents report weeds or other code issues through dispatch at 575-526-0975 or an online non-emergency portal, and the city publishes a public map of properties on its nuisance list. According to the city, a condemned property is one judged unfit for occupancy, and condemnation does not mean the city is taking the building or tearing it down. Owners are invited to contact Community Development about abatement options and permits for repair or demolition.

If your house is on that list, or if a neighbor has complained about it, deal with it before you sell. A cash buyer can take a house with open code issues, though the title company will want to know about any liens or fines.

How do Doña Ana County taxes, protests and exemptions work for a seller?

Doña Ana County follows the same calendar as the rest of New Mexico: tax bills are mailed by November 1, the first half is due November 10 and delinquent after December 10, and the second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10. Delinquent taxes accrue 1 percent interest each month, plus a 1 percent penalty for up to five months with a $5 minimum, and the county says no one can waive them once accrued.

The county's own example for a Las Cruces home appraised at $100,000, with a head of household deduction of $2,000 and a mill levy of 0.029269, comes to $917.10 in tax. That is an illustration, not your bill.

Points from the Treasurer's FAQ that affect a sale:

  • Taxes cannot be prorated by the county. The owner of record on January 1 is responsible for that year's tax, and a lien attaches if it goes unpaid, whoever owns the house later. Buyer and seller usually split the bill through the title company.
  • A valuation protest goes to the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value, usually in April. Missing it leaves a refund claim in District Court after paying by December 10 and filing by January 10.
  • New Mexico has no homestead exemption. It has a head of family exemption, and a valuation freeze for owners who are 65 or older, or disabled, with modified gross income under $35,000.
  • A mobile home needs a property tax release from the Assessor, paid by cash, cashier's check or money order, before title can transfer.

Real property with three or more years of delinquent taxes can be sold at a state auction unless all years are paid, which is why back taxes should be resolved before or at closing.

What do schools, roads and utilities look like, and which sale route fits?

The Las Cruces Public School District covers the city, White Sands Missile Range, the settlement of Doña Ana and the town of Mesilla, with 26 elementary schools, nine middle schools and six high schools, per Wikipedia. Interstate 10 and Interstate 25 meet here, and Las Cruces is the southern end of I-25. RoadRUNNER Transit runs eight routes plus two Aggie routes, and Las Cruces International Airport has service to Albuquerque on Advanced Air.

The city provides water, sewer, natural gas and solid waste service, and El Paso Electric supplies power. Final bills and meter readings are a closing-day task.

You can list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or take a cash offer. A listing may bring the best price for a house in good shape. A cash sale can fit a vacant house facing the registry fee, a probate property, a rental with a difficult tenant, or a house that needs more repair than you can fund. We do not promise a price. Get any offer in writing, confirm who pays closing costs, and use a title company for the transfer.

More questions about Las Cruces, NM

When are Doña Ana County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 and delinquent after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10. Bills are mailed by November 1.

Do I need to register a vacant house in Las Cruces?

If the building has not been lawfully occupied or in operation for at least two consecutive years, it may qualify under the city's vacant and abandoned property ordinance and need annual registration. Fees for a residential house start at $500 in year one. Contact the city at Vacancy@LasCruces.gov.

Can I get an exemption from the vacancy fee if I am selling?

The city lists exemptions for active sale or lease marketing that meets its pricing and marketing requirements, among others. They need city approval and last 12 months.

Can I protest my Las Cruces property valuation?

Yes. File a protest with the Doña Ana County Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value, usually in April. If you miss it, you can pay by December 10 and file a refund claim in District Court by January 10.

Does New Mexico have a homestead exemption?

No, according to the county Treasurer. It offers a head of family exemption for owner-occupied primary residences and a valuation freeze for qualifying owners age 65 or older or disabled.

What happens if the house has code violations?

The Nuisance Abatement Team and Code Enforcement handle problem properties under the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code. You can still sell, but fines or liens will need to be dealt with at closing.

Where is Rio Rancho and how is the city laid out?

Rio Rancho sits in the Albuquerque Basin of central New Mexico, mostly in Sandoval County with a small northern slice of Bernalillo County. It is the largest city in Sandoval County and part of the Albuquerque metro area.

The city covers about 103.7 square miles, and the Rio Grande forms a boundary at its northeast corner. An escarpment rises to the west of the city limit. Albuquerque lies to the south, Santa Ana Pueblo to the north, and the town of Bernalillo and the village of Corrales to the east. The elevation is about 5,509 feet.

For a seller, the practical point is that two counties can touch a Rio Rancho address. Most homes are billed by Sandoval County, but a property in the Bernalillo County portion deals with a different assessor and treasurer. Check which county your tax bill comes from before you call any office.

How did Rio Rancho grow, and what does that mean for a house here?

Rio Rancho began as a planned land-sales community. In 1961 the AMREP Corporation bought about 55,000 acres and created a housing development called Rio Rancho Estates, and the first families arrived in the early 1960s. The city was incorporated in 1981, the same year an Intel plant opened and added many jobs.

The population grew ten-fold between 1970 and 1980, and the city has kept growing since. That means a seller may own an older house on a street where neighbors have much newer ones, and a buyer will ask about the age of the roof and major systems on either.

After the 2008 housing collapse, foreclosure activity rose in the city, and Sandoval, Bernalillo and Valencia counties all felt the recession. The city later adopted an abandoned residential property registration ordinance, covered in the rules section below.

What drives the Rio Rancho economy?

Intel is the largest employer in Rio Rancho, followed by the public school district and a hospital. A 2026 Albuquerque Business First list of Rio Rancho-area employers shows the top four:

EmployerRio Rancho employeesNote
Intel Corp.3,100Semiconductor manufacturing, founded locally in 1980
Rio Rancho Public Schools2,830About 15,500 students
Presbyterian Rust Medical Center1,250210-bed acute care hospital
City of Rio Rancho796Municipal government

The same article notes that Intel employment in Rio Rancho has dropped, though the company still tops the list. Intel's Fab 11X, a 300mm wafer plant, opened in 2002. A strong link to one large employer means local home demand can follow that employer's news, so sellers should not assume the past will repeat.

Retail, services and government round out the local economy. The Downtown City Centre area holds City Hall, a University of New Mexico West and Central New Mexico Community College campus, and the Santa Ana Star Center arena.

What does Rio Rancho's dry climate mean for a house?

Rio Rancho has an arid climate and averages about 8.90 inches of precipitation a year. The city sits in the rain shadow of the Sandia Mountains to the east and the Continental Divide to the west. The higher western part of the city gets slightly more rain and snow than the denser eastern side.

Low rainfall does not remove the need for an inspection. A buyer's inspector will still look at the roof, drainage around the foundation, and any exterior finish. If you plan to sell to an investor or cash buyer instead, those items are priced into the offer, and you can skip repairs.

Which schools and roads serve Rio Rancho?

Rio Rancho Public Schools serves most of the city, with Rio Rancho High School and V. Sue Cleveland High School as its two major public high schools. Parts of the city fall in the Jemez Valley Public Schools district, and much of the Bernalillo County portion is zoned to Albuquerque Public Schools. Two public charter schools, The ASK Academy and Cyber Academy, serve grades 6 to 12.

Buyers often start with the school district boundary, so confirm which district your address belongs to before you describe it in a listing or to a buyer.

  • Albuquerque's ABQ RIDE operates route 251, which connects Rio Rancho to the Rail Runner station at Journal Center.
  • Rio Metro RTD runs a commuter bus for the Enchanted Hills neighborhood to the US 550 Rail Runner station, and a route toward Cuba with a park and ride near NM 528 and NM 550.
  • Residents can also reach Albuquerque by road, since the city borders it to the south.

What city rules affect a Rio Rancho home sale?

Three Rio Rancho rules come up most often for sellers: permits, short-term rentals and abandoned property registration.

Permits. The city's Building Division issues permits and inspects construction, and the city advises calling the permit office at 505-891-5005 before starting a home project to ask if a permit is required. The city lists the 2021 International Residential Code among its governing codes. Unpermitted work done by a past owner can come up during a sale, so gather any permit records you have.

Short-term rentals. Since July 1, 2025, a permit is required to operate, rent, offer to rent or advertise a short-term rental in the city. The city defines it as a stay of less than 30 days in a single-family residence. A 5% Lodgers' Tax applies. Development Services can fine up to $500 per day for violations. If your house was used this way, the new owner needs their own permit, so tell the buyer early.

Abandoned property. The Governing Body approved an Abandoned Residential Property Registration ordinance in December 2011. If a house is vacant after an owner dies or moves out, read the ordinance on the city's Code Enforcement pages. We could not confirm the registration deadlines or fees, so check with the city directly.

How do Sandoval County property taxes work when you sell?

Sandoval County values the property, and the Sandoval County Treasurer collects the tax. The assessor mails a Notice of Value by April 1 each year, and you have 30 days from mailing to protest. The notice is not a bill.

DateWhat happens
January 1Property is assessed to the owner of record, and taxes are a lien from this date
April 1Notice of Value is due to be mailed
30 days after mailingLast day to file a valuation protest or claim an exemption
November 1Tax bills mailed
November 10 and December 10First half due, then delinquent after December 10
April 10 and May 10Second half due, then delinquent after May 10

Taxable value is one-third of assessed value, minus exemptions. New Mexico has no homestead exemption. It has a Head of Family exemption, which Sandoval County describes as $2,000 off taxable value for a primary residence. If a property changes hands after January 1, that exemption is removed the next January 1, and the new owner must apply.

A deed must be recorded with the county clerk before the assessor updates the owner. If you close with a title company, it records the deed for you. Taxes unpaid for two years can lead to a state auction, so a seller with old balances should settle them or sell before then. The county's office is the Sandoval County Assessor FAQ page.

What are your options for selling a Rio Rancho house?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. Each route differs in timing, cost and effort.

  • List with an agent: usually gives the widest exposure, and you handle showings, inspections and any repair requests.
  • Sell it yourself: saves a commission but leaves marketing, paperwork and negotiation to you.
  • Cash offer: a buyer purchases the house as it stands, so repairs and cleaning are not part of your job. Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, and compare it with what you would net after costs on the other two routes.

A cash sale can suit sellers in a few common Rio Rancho situations: an inherited house, back payments, a rental with tenants, or a house that needs work. Before you sign, ask the title company how property tax and any liens will be handled at closing, and keep copies of every document.

More questions about Rio Rancho, NM

How many people live in Rio Rancho?

The Census Bureau estimates 114,419 residents as of July 1, 2025, and the 2020 census counted 104,046. It is the largest city in Sandoval County.

Which county is Rio Rancho in?

Most of Rio Rancho is in Sandoval County, and a small northern portion extends into Bernalillo County. Your tax bill shows which county's assessor and treasurer handle your property.

When are Sandoval County property taxes due?

Bills are mailed by November 1. The first half is due November 10 and becomes delinquent after December 10, and the second half is due April 10 and becomes delinquent after May 10, according to the Sandoval County Assessor.

Do I need a permit to run a short-term rental in Rio Rancho?

Yes. Since July 1, 2025, a short-term rental permit is required to operate, rent or advertise one in the city, and a 5% Lodgers' Tax applies. Fines can reach $500 per day.

Can I sell a Rio Rancho house that needs repairs?

Yes. You can sell it as-is to a cash buyer, or list it and negotiate repairs with a buyer after inspection. Compare the net amount from each route.

Where is Santa Fe and why is it different from other New Mexico cities?

Santa Fe is the capital of New Mexico and the county seat of Santa Fe County. It lies at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains at 6,998 feet, the highest elevation of any U.S. state capital.

The city covers about 52.4 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 87,505 residents. Founded in 1610 as the capital of Nuevo México, it is the oldest state capital in the United States. It became capital of the U.S. Territory of New Mexico in 1851 and the state capital in 1912.

That age shows up in the housing. Santa Fe is known for adobe-style Pueblo Revival and Territorial Revival architecture, much of it preserved and protected, so a seller here may own a house shaped by rules that do not apply in other cities.

What does the Santa Fe economy look like?

Government is the largest employer in Santa Fe, with roughly 15,000 jobs, followed by education and health services and by leisure and hospitality.

Tourism and the arts are central. The city has more than 250 art galleries and hosts the Santa Fe International Folk Art Market, the Traditional Spanish Colonial Market and Indian Market. About one-tenth of all employment is tied to artistic and cultural industries. Los Alamos National Laboratory is about a 45-minute drive away.

Because so many jobs depend on the state government and visitors, local demand can shift with budgets and travel seasons, and a seller should ask any buyer how long they need to close.

What is the wider Santa Fe region?

The Santa Fe metropolitan area has an estimated 158,000 people, and the greater Albuquerque, Santa Fe and Los Alamos combined statistical area spans eight counties and 1.16 million residents.

Santa Fe Plaza, the Palace of the Governors and the Santa Fe Historic District anchor the center, and the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum and Meow Wolf are among its cultural draws. In 2005 Santa Fe became the first U.S. city inducted into the UNESCO Creative Cities Network.

The Rail Runner Express serves the city through four stations: Santa Fe Depot, South Capitol, Zia Road and Santa Fe County/NM 599.

How does Santa Fe's climate affect a house?

Santa Fe averages 12.79 inches of precipitation and 20.2 inches of snow a year. The 24-hour average temperature runs from 30.3°F in December to 70.1°F in July, so heating is a real cost for much of the year.

Wildfire is also a local concern. The Santa Fe Fire Department says it is one of the only fire departments in New Mexico with ten full-time employees who specialize in fuel management in the Wildland Urban Interface. It offers free Wildfire Home Hazard Assessments and evacuation zone information. If your house backs onto open land, an assessment report can show a buyer what you have done.

  • Ask the fire department for a home hazard assessment before listing.
  • Keep records of any brush clearing or roof work.
  • Check your homeowner insurance terms, since buyers ask about them.

What historic district rules apply when selling in Santa Fe?

Santa Fe has five historic districts, and the Historic Districts Review Board (HDRB) reviews alterations that cannot be approved by staff. The board is a quasi-judicial body that designates historic status of structures, approves new construction and reviews changes to existing ones. The city lists its meetings for the second and fourth Tuesday of the month.

The city's Historic Preservation Division says it preserves the character of Santa Fe by administering the Historic Districts and Archaeological Districts ordinances. A buyer who wants to change a front facade, windows or walls in a district may need review first.

If your house sits in one of the districts, tell any buyer early, and ask the Historic Preservation Division what is on file for the address. The division lists historicpreservation@santafenm.gov for questions and hpdsubmittal@santafenm.gov for submittals, so you can ask what has been approved or filed for your address in writing. Because we could not confirm the exact boundaries of each district, confirm yours with the city.

What other Santa Fe rules affect a home sale?

The most common city rule for sellers is the short-term rental permit. Santa Fe requires every short-term rental to hold a business registration and either a Residential Short-Term Rental Permit or a Non-Residential Short-Term Rental Registration, depending on zoning. Anyone planning to own or run a short-term rental in calendar year 2026 must obtain a permit, and within 10 days of issuance or renewal the owner must notify required parties by first-class mail.

If your house has run as a rental, hand the buyer the permit status in writing. A new owner cannot assume the permit is theirs without checking the city's rules.

Schools are covered by Santa Fe Public Schools. Interstate 25, U.S. 84, U.S. 285 and NM 599 serve the city, and the Rail Runner Express stops at four Santa Fe stations. Santa Fe Regional Airport handles local flights.

How do Santa Fe County property taxes work?

The Santa Fe County Assessor values property and the Santa Fe County Treasurer collects the tax. The treasurer sends about 60,000 real property, personal property and mobile home tax bills each year.

In 2026 the county said a change from House Bill 285 widens the disabled veterans' exemption, so veterans with a service-connected disability rating below 100% are now eligible for a portion of it. If you are selling a house that carried this exemption, ask the assessor how the exemption transfers.

The treasurer's site lists a card fee of 2.5% and a flat $1.95 e-check fee on its payment platforms, so ask how a payment at closing will be made before you assume a method.

What are your options for selling a house fast in Santa Fe?

A Santa Fe seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer.

  • List with an agent: gives wide exposure but may involve inspections, repair requests and staging for a Santa Fe buyer.
  • Sell on your own: saves a commission but leaves paperwork and negotiation to you.
  • Cash offer: from a buyer who buys the house as it stands. Ask for the offer in writing and read it closely.

Cash sales often fit owners who inherited a house, hold a vacant second home, or face repairs on an older adobe. Whichever route you pick, gather the tax bill, any HDRB paperwork, rental permits and repair records before you talk to a buyer.

Santa Fe is in Santa Fe County, and it is the county seat as well as the state capital.

Bills are mailed on or before November 1. The first half is due November 10 and becomes delinquent after December 10, and the second half is due on or before May 10.

Do I need a permit to run a short-term rental in Santa Fe?

Yes. Every short-term rental needs a business registration and a permit or registration, depending on zoning, and an owner who plans to operate in 2026 must obtain an STR permit.

Can I sell a Santa Fe house as-is?

Yes. A cash buyer buys as-is, and a listed sale can also close without repairs if the buyer agrees. Compare what you would net on each route.

Where is Roswell and what is the city like?

Roswell is the county seat of Chaves County in southeastern New Mexico. It sits at about 3,615 feet, roughly 7 miles west of the Pecos River, with highlands rising toward the Sierra Blanca range some 40 miles to the west.

The city covers just under 30 square miles. It was founded in 1871 and incorporated on February 25, 1889, and the 2020 census counted 48,422 residents, which made it the fifth most populous city in the state. Chaves County makes up the whole Roswell micropolitan area, so the city is the regional center for shopping, health care and county government.

U.S. Routes 70, 285 and 380 pass through, and the Roswell International Air Center is the local airport. For a seller, the main effect of this setting is a smaller, more local pool of buyers than in a big metro. Local employers and the military school and college campuses shape who looks for a house here.

What is Roswell's history, and why does it matter to a home seller?

Roswell was a place of military importance from 1941 to 1967, and Walker Air Force Base was decommissioned in 1967. The Roswell Army Air Field handled the investigation and debris recovery for the 1947 incident that made the city's name famous, although the crash site was some 75 miles north near Corona.

In the 1930s, Robert H. Goddard did much of his early rocketry work in Roswell, and Goddard High School carries his name. Since 1997, an annual UFO Festival has marked the 50th anniversary of the 1947 event.

Why this matters when you sell: Roswell has been a settled city for well over a century, so many houses are old. An older house may have original wiring, plumbing or heating, and buyers and lenders ask about them. A cash buyer will usually take such a house as it is.

What drives the Roswell economy?

Roswell's economy mixes irrigated farming, dairying and ranching with manufacturing, distribution, petroleum-related facilities, education and tourism. A Leprino Foods mozzarella plant is among the best known manufacturers.

Tourism rests on ufology museums, including the International UFO Museum and Research Center, plus Americana travel. Bitter Lake National Wildlife Refuge lies a few miles northeast of the city, and Bottomless Lakes State Park is 12 miles east on U.S. 380.

How does Roswell's climate and flood history affect a house?

Roswell has a cold semi-arid climate with four distinct seasons. It averages 11.63 inches of precipitation a year and 9.6 inches of snow. The mean daily high runs from 56.5°F in December to 96.5°F in July, and the record range is from minus 24°F to 114°F. Heating and cooling systems both matter to a buyer.

Summer monsoon storms can bring torrential downpours, severe thunderstorms and sometimes tornadoes. Roswell also has a flood history from the Rio Hondo. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers records mass flooding in 1937, 1941 and 1954, which led to a flood control facility at Two Rivers Dam. The city posts FEMA flood information, including a March 23, 2012 map revision that shows dramatic changes to Hondo River floodplains.

  • Check the FEMA flood map for your address before you list.
  • Ask your insurance agent whether the home sits in a mapped floodplain.

The Roswell Independent School District serves the city, and Goddard High School is named for the rocket scientist. Roswell is also home to NMMI and an ENMU branch campus.

Code enforcement. The city's Code Enforcement Department works to keep Roswell a desirable place to live and do business. A City Council agenda from 2026 shows the council declaring structures to be dangerous buildings and public nuisances under Roswell Municipal Code section 16-12. If your house is vacant, damaged or neglected, a code complaint can reach you before a sale does, so clear any open notice first.

Permits. The city runs an online system for residential permits, with applications, email updates and inspection requests. Ask the city whether past work at your address was permitted.

How do Chaves County property taxes work in Roswell?

Chaves County handles property tax for Roswell addresses. Taxes go to several agencies, including the State of New Mexico, Chaves County, the Roswell Independent School District, ENMU-Roswell, the City of Roswell and the Flood Control Conservancy District.

Each county holds an annual auction in its commission chambers.

The Chaves County Assessor's office is at 1 St Mary's Place in Roswell, and the county's main number is 575-624-6600. A statewide rule gives owners 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed to protest the value, and New Mexico's 2026 House Bill 285 restates that protest wording in the property tax code.

Under New Mexico law as summarized by Sandoval County, property taxes are a lien from January 1 of the tax year, and the owner of record on that date is responsible for that year's tax. If you sell in the spring, the buyer and seller usually settle the current year's tax through the contract, so ask the title company to show you how it is split on the closing statement.

What should a Roswell seller gather before talking to a buyer?

A short folder of documents speeds up any sale, whether it is a listing or a cash purchase.

  • Your latest Chaves County tax bill and proof of payment for both halves.
  • Any code enforcement notice, with the date and what it asked you to fix.
  • Receipts or permits for roof, plumbing, heating or storm repairs.
  • The FEMA flood zone for the address and any flood insurance policy.
  • For an inherited house, the death certificate and the probate or title paperwork.

Having these on hand lets a buyer give you a clear number sooner, and it protects you from surprises at the closing table.

What are your options for selling a Roswell house fast?

A Roswell owner can list the house, sell it directly, or take a cash offer, and the right choice depends on condition, timing and cost.

  • Direct sale: avoids an agent but needs you to handle price, contract and paperwork.

Common reasons Roswell owners look at a cash sale are an inherited house, a vacant property attracting code notices, a flood or storm repair, tenants, or taxes that have fallen behind. Whatever route you choose, ask the title company how taxes and liens are handled at closing.

Roswell is in Chaves County and is its county seat. Chaves County forms the entire Roswell micropolitan area.

Where is Farmington, and what is the setting like?

Farmington sits in the northwest corner of New Mexico at the meeting point of the San Juan, Animas and La Plata rivers, on the Colorado Plateau. The Navajo name for the place, Tóta', means where three rivers meet.

It is the largest city in San Juan County, a county of 5,538 square miles, and Wikipedia describes it as the commercial hub for northwestern New Mexico and the Four Corners area. The city covers about 32 square miles, at an elevation of 5,473 feet. The 2020 census counted 46,624 residents.

Main roads are US 64, which crosses the city east to west, NM 170 to the north, NM 371 to the south toward Interstate 40, and NM 516 toward Aztec and US 550. Four Corners Regional Airport handles flights. Because three rivers meet here, flood maps and insurance are worth a look, which we cover below.

How did Farmington grow, and what does that history mean for houses?

Farmington grew in bursts tied to transport and energy. Ancestral Pueblo people lived in the area from the 7th century, and after the Navajo Nation was created in 1868 the rest of the county opened to settlers from southern Colorado, who first called the place Junction City. The town incorporated as Farmington in 1901.

A railroad connecting it to Durango, Colorado was finished in September 1905. Oil and gas investment came in the 1920s, though output stayed low until the 1950s. After the 1940s a developed road linked the town to US Route 66 and Albuquerque, and the San Juan Basin natural gas pipeline followed in 1953, and population rose quickly.

Wikipedia notes that the town's reliance on energy left it exposed to price swings during the 1970s crisis and pushed some diversification. Owners who bought during a boom and sell during a slowdown feel that history directly.

What happened to the coal plant, and how does it affect a Farmington sale?

The San Juan Generating Station near Farmington closed in 2022, and the nearby San Juan coal mine closed with it. San Juan Citizens Alliance reports that the owners, led by Public Service Company of New Mexico, retired the last two units that year, that the smokestacks were imploded in August 2024, and that demolition and reclamation continue.

The same group says the plant once generated 1,600 megawatts, that the Four Corners Power Plant is slated for retirement in 2031, and that PNM is bonding up to $40 million under the 2019 Energy Transition Act for economic development, workforce retraining and severance in the Four Corners region. PNM is buying power from the San Juan Solar project, which includes 200 megawatts of solar and 100 megawatts of battery storage.

We cite an advocacy group here, so treat its framing with care. The facts that matter to a seller are simple:

  • A major power plant and its mine have closed, and a second plant is scheduled to retire in 2031.
  • Replacement spending is tied to solar projects, retraining funds and economic development programs.
  • Buyers and lenders look at local job stability when they weigh a purchase.

If a job change or a layoff is the reason you need to sell, a faster closing can help you avoid more months of payments on a house that may sit on the market.

What are winters, summers and storms like for a Farmington house?

Farmington has a semi-arid climate with cold winters and hot summers. NOAA normals on Wikipedia show a January mean daily low of 20 degrees and a July mean daily high of about 90, with annual precipitation near 8 inches. The record low is minus 34 degrees and the record high is 105.

That temperature swing, rather than rain, is what a buyer's inspector looks at. Pipes in crawl spaces and exterior walls face freezing weather, roofs and decks face strong sun, and heating and cooling equipment both run hard. Snowfall is modest; the table gives 8.6 inches a year.

Flooding is a separate matter. The county Treasurer's FAQ page carried a flooding update banner when we read it, pointing to county emergency management for the latest on the San Juan and Animas rivers. If your house is near either river, check the FEMA flood map for the address and ask your insurer what coverage applies before you list. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance for a house in a mapped flood zone, and that can change who will buy it and when.

How do San Juan County property taxes work for a Farmington seller?

San Juan County mails tax bills by November 1, and the full amount or the first half is due November 10. The county says taxes become delinquent if unpaid by close of business December 10, and the second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10.

The county explains that taxable value is one third of full value, and that the State Department of Finance and Administration sets the tax rate each September from budgets submitted by the county, schools, cities and voter-approved bonds. If a bill totals less than $5, the county adds an administrative fee to bring it to $5. Late payment adds 1 percent interest and 1 percent penalty per month, with the penalty alone capped at 5 percent.

If a sale closes after the late August cutoff, the old owner may still receive the next bill. Ask your title company who is paying what, and watch your mail for a notice sent in the previous owner's name.

What else changes the tax bill when a Farmington house sells?

The county's FAQ gives several details that come up during sales. If a house is sold on a real estate contract, the previous owner's name stays on the bill, with the buyer's name after "C/O," until the contract is paid off. A buyer with a recorded deed should take it to the Assessor's office to confirm the tax roll.

If a mortgage company pays taxes through escrow, the bill still goes to the owner, with a box marked to show that the lender requested the bill. An old escrow account may use a wrong account number, and the county asks owners to call right away if the box is marked and no lender is involved.

A seller should do these things before closing:

  • Pull the most recent bill and confirm both halves are paid.
  • Ask the title company whether the buyer is taking over escrow or paying cash.
  • Check that the Assessor has your correct mailing address so a notice of value reaches you.
  • Keep copies of every payment receipt.

Not receiving a notice of value or a bill does not remove the obligation, according to the county.

Who is buying in Farmington, and which sale routes are open?

Schools are one factor buyers weigh. Farmington Municipal Schools serves over 10,000 students in 20 schools, with Farmington High, Piedra Vista High and Rocinante High among its high schools, and San Juan College is a public two-year college with a headcount of almost 6,000 in fall 2021, per Wikipedia.

The city also owns its electric utility, the Farmington Electric Utility System, which serves roughly 46,000 metered customers across a service area that reaches beyond the city limits. A buyer comparing a house in the city with one just outside may see different utility arrangements.

You have three routes: list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or sell for cash to a company like ours. Listing may produce the highest price for a house in good repair, though it requires showings, repair credits and a financing contingency. A direct sale suits owners with inherited property, back taxes, tenants, or a house with deferred maintenance. We make no promise about a price, and any offer will depend on the property, its location and its needs.

Before you accept any offer, get it in writing, confirm who pays closing costs and who holds earnest money, and have a title company handle the closing.

Bills are mailed by November 1. The full amount or the first half is due November 10 and becomes delinquent after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and becomes delinquent after May 10.

Who pays property tax if I sell my Farmington house mid-year?

By state statute the owner on January 1 is responsible, though buyer and seller usually divide the year at closing through the title company. Ask for the split in writing.

Can I sell a Farmington house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax, interest and penalty are usually paid from sale proceeds at closing. Call the County Treasurer at (505) 334-9421 for a current balance.

Does the closing of the San Juan Generating Station make it harder to sell?

It changed the local job base, and some owners are selling after job changes. Whether it affects your sale depends on the neighborhood and the condition of the house.

How do I check whether my Farmington house is in a flood zone?

Use the FEMA flood map for your address and ask your insurer. If the property is near the San Juan or Animas river, check before you list, since a lender may require flood insurance.

Who updates the owner name or address on the tax roll?

The County Assessor. The Treasurer collects taxes but cannot change the tax roll without the Assessor's authorization or a court order.

How did oil shape Hobbs?

Hobbs began as a homestead in 1907 and became an oil town after the Midwest Oil Company found oil in 1927. A refinery opened the next year, and the town incorporated in 1929. At the peak of that first boom more than 12,000 people lived there.

The Depression ended the boom for a time. Oil prices fell and the population dropped to about 3,000 by 1931, then climbed back to about 14,000 by 1940 as drilling picked up. A Hobbs Army Airfield was built in 1942, and in 1948 the city bought the air base and turned it into the Hobbs Industrial Air Park, still used for soaring competitions.

That swing from 12,000 to 3,000 and back is worth keeping in mind. The population here has followed oil activity, and an owner who bought near a peak may want to sell in a quieter year. More recently, the Energy Information Administration reports that Lea and Eddy counties together accounted for nearly 1.0 million barrels a day, or 52 percent, of U.S. crude oil production growth between 2020 and 2024.

Who are the major employers and what does that mean for housing?

Wikipedia lists mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction as the largest industries in Hobbs, followed by retail trade and educational services. Nearby Eunice hosts a uranium enrichment facility operated by Urenco USA, which provides technician and nuclear engineering jobs across the region, including Hobbs.

Other anchors include Hobbs Municipal Schools, the University of the Southwest, a private four-year Christian university, and New Mexico Junior College, a public two-year college that opened in 1966. Zia Park, a racetrack and casino with a 154-room hotel, is in town, and the Soaring Society of America has its headquarters here.

  • Oil and gas extraction is the largest industry, so local demand is tied to energy activity.
  • Schools, colleges and retail add employment that does not depend on drilling.
  • The Urenco enrichment plant in nearby Eunice draws technical workers to the area.

Ask any buyer or agent how current oilfield activity is affecting demand in your part of town.

What flood and weather risks should a Hobbs seller disclose to a buyer?

The City of Hobbs says flooding is one of the biggest hazards in the greater Hobbs area and can happen with little or no notice. It also lists severe weather, extreme heat and drought, grass fires and power outages as hazards.

The city has taken part in the National Flood Insurance Program and the Community Rating System since 1992. It is a Class 8 community, which the city says saves residents 10 percent on flood insurance premiums. If a flood zone touches a property line, the city notes that insurance may be cheaper, though not required. Land drains east toward Seminole Draw or southeast toward Monument Draw, so water follows the low points.

Hobbs also keeps copies of elevation certificates, which a buyer may need for insurance if the house sits in a Special Flood Hazard Area. The Engineering Department can be reached at (575) 397-9232. The city's page also says that thunderstorms, hail, lightning, tornadoes and wind-driven grass fires happen on the high plains. Summer highs average in the mid 90s, and annual precipitation is about 12 inches by the city's count, close to the 13.77 inches NOAA reports.

Gather these before listing:

  • FEMA flood zone for the address
  • Any elevation certificate on file with the city
  • Roof age and hail or wind repair records
  • Flood or storm insurance claims in the past

What permits and codes apply to a Hobbs house?

The city's Building Safety and Permitting office, part of the Planning and Engineering Department, issues permits for building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work on residential and commercial property. It is at 200 E. Broadway Street, phone (575) 391-8158.

The office lists permits for new buildings, additions, remodels, demolitions, manufactured homes, re-roofs, HVAC, fireplaces, pools, decks, fences and curb cuts. It publishes residential re-roofing guidelines and a homeowner building permit application. Current state codes it lists include the 2021 New Mexico Residential Building Code, effective January 1, 2024.

For a seller, the useful question is whether work done on the house since you bought it had a permit. A buyer's inspector may ask. If you did a re-roof, a deck or a bathroom remodel without paperwork, ask the office what is needed to close the file, or tell a cash buyer up front so the price reflects it. The city's contact page lists Code Enforcement at (575) 391-4178.

Three highways, US 60, US 70 and US 84, run through town. Four things carry most of the local economy: Cannon Air Force Base, the BNSF rail yard, agriculture and dairy processing, and a small group of manufacturers. When one of them shifts, house sales in Clovis tend to feel it.

Spring brings frequent severe thunderstorms, and summer evenings bring heavy rain. Winter snow tends to arrive for several weeks in January and February. The statute lists transfers that do not count as a change of ownership, such as certain transfers between spouses, to a child who lives in the home, or into a revocable trust. The city runs a 311 portal called Clovis NM Works for non-emergency problems, and neighbors can use it to report nuisances such as debris in alleys or overgrown lots. Reports can be anonymous and can include a photo.

If you have an inherited or vacant house, check that no open complaint is attached to the address before you list. Who buys houses in Clovis, and which sale route fits which situation?

Buyers in Clovis fall into three groups: military households, local families, and investors who rent to both. Each group wants something different from a listing.

A military buyer using a VA loan faces an appraisal and condition review, which can be harder for a house with a failing roof or foundation movement. A local family may rely on a bank loan and a standard inspection. An investor or cash buyer can close on a shorter timeline and accept the house in its present state.

Selling on the open market can bring the highest price for a clean, updated house, but it also brings showings, inspection requests, appraisal risk and agent commission. A cash sale trades some of that price for speed and certainty. A direct sale suits a seller facing probate, a move on orders, tax debt, a tenant who will not leave, or repairs the family cannot pay for.

The settlement was christened Eddy on September 15, 1888, after Charles B. Eddy of the Eddy-Bissell Livestock Company, and was organized as a municipal corporation in 1893. The town later voted to change its name to Carlsbad, after the European spa Karlsbad in Bohemia, because of its mineral springs.

Most of the water inside city limits is the Pecos River and the Lake Carlsbad recreation area, which together make up 0.93 percent of the city's area. Cavern City Air Terminal sits just south of town. Wikipedia reports Contour Airlines offering non-stop service to Albuquerque and Denver, which a relocating owner may find useful for scheduling a closing from out of town.

Wikipedia reports about 89 days a year above 90 degrees Fahrenheit. Buyers' inspectors usually look closely at cooling equipment and roofs for that reason.

Who values property for tax in Alamogordo?

The Otero County Assessor values it and the Otero County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. The city does not run a separate property tax bill.
